newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwandan defendant arrives at genocide tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan defendant arrives at genocide tribunal.

text.p: A Rwandan Hutu accused of genocide during the mass slaughter in Rwanda in 1994 arrived on Thursday at court in northern Tanzania for the resumption of his trial.
Jean Paul Akayesu, in handcuffs, was escorted under tight security into the headquarters of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
The white U.N. van bringing him from a Tanzanian prison bumped into another vehicle while Akayesu was being unloaded but he was not hurt. Wearing a dark suit, he was led into the court building.

Akayesu, 43, a former government official in Taba commune in central Rwanda has pleaded not guilty to charges of crimes against humanity and genocide during the killing of up to a million Rwandan Tutsis and Hutu political moderates in 1994.
An American lawyer for Akayesu said he would seek a seven-month postponement in court on Thursday of the case because he still needed time to interview witnesses in Zaire and Rwanda.
A U.N. official is in Arusha investigating the tribunal amid charges that the slow-moving judicial process to bring to justice leaders of the 1994 genocide has been paralysed by its own staff.
Speaking on Wednesday, the information chief for the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda accused Acting Administration Chief George Anderson, a Liberian, of obstructing activity.

"Things have been paralysed by the acting chief of administration. The investigation is ongoing," said Beatrice Lacoste, confirming an investigator from the U.N. inspector general's office had arrived at the tribunal's headquarters.
In New York, Karl Paschke, U.N. undersecretary-general for internal oversight services, told reporters on Wednesday:

"I can confirm to you that we are at present reviewing the situation both in Kigali and Arusha on the basis of a number of reports my office has received in the recent past. I have fielded a team of auditors and a field of investigators."
"Yes, we've had problems at the tribunal," Lacoste told Reuters in Arusha. "There's no question there are problems in administration. More red tape than there should be."
She said the tribunal suffered from a lack of publicity for trials leading to a poor image, problems over getting equipment that caused delays and administrative problems.
Tribunal staff have complained in the past about incompetence among fellow staff, U.N. politics and bureaucracy.
The tribunal, with a budget of $36 million this year, indicted 21 suspects of whom 12 are in custody. Judges had hoped trials in Arusha would show the world mass killings would not go unpunished.
But Akayesu's appearance in court on Thursday has largely been overshadowed by new ethnic conflict in eastern Zaire uprooting more than 500,000 Rwandan Hutu and Burundian refugees.
